questions.prompt: A school library holds 600 books; the library of the village next door holds 200. Which sentence compares them the way this module does?

options.text: The school library has three times as many books as the village one.
The school library has three times as many books than the village one.
The school library has three times as much books as the village one.
The school library has three times more books as the village one.

questions.explanation: A comparison of scale is built as multiplier + as + many or much + noun + as, and 600 against 200 gives the multiplier three times: three times as many books as. "three times as many books than the village one" replaces the second as with than, which belongs to an ordinary comparative, not to this structure. "three times as much books" puts much in front of a noun you can count; books takes many. "three times more books as" builds the sentence on more, which then demands than and gives a different claim altogether, since three times more than can be read as four times as many.

questions.prompt: Two gaps need the same kind of word: "An online course gives you ___ more freedom." and "A campus gives you ___ more friends." Which pair fills them?
questions.explanation: The noun decides, not the comparison. freedom cannot be counted, so it takes much more; friends can be counted, so they take many more. That gives much … many. The reversed pair puts many in front of an uncountable noun and much in front of a countable one, which is exactly the mistake the module warns against; the two uniform pairs get one of the two gaps wrong for the same reason.

questions.prompt: A pupil is told that he may not come back to the school at all, and that his family must find him another school or another way of studying. Which of the four punishments of the module is that?
questions.explanation: Exclusion is the heaviest of the four: the pupil does not come back, and another school or another form of education has to be found. Suspension is the one that stops short of it — the pupil attends no lesson, but only until the school has met about his case. Detention keeps him back at the end of the day or calls him in on Sunday, and lines cost him nothing but a page of copying.

questions.prompt: A journalist's notebook keeps only this line of an interview: "I asked her whether she spoke any foreign languages." Which question did the journalist actually put to her?
questions.explanation: Two clues fix the original. The reported question opens on whether, so it was a yes/no question and not a question built on a WH word — which rules out "Which foreign languages do you speak?", whose report would have kept which. And after a past reporting verb the simple present moves back to the simple past, so spoke comes from speak: "Do you speak any foreign languages?" The present continuous would have given was speaking, and the simple past would have given had spoken.

questions.prompt: Two versions of one sentence about a class: "The pupils who sat at the back never opened a book." and "The pupils, who sat at the back, never opened a book." What does the second version say that the first does not?

options.text: That every one of the pupils sat at the back.
That only some of the pupils never opened a book.
That the pupils opened a book at the back.
That the teacher sat at the back with them.

questions.explanation: The two commas turn the clause into a non-restrictive one: it no longer selects anybody, it simply adds a detail about the whole group, so all the pupils sat at the back and none of them ever opened a book. Without the commas the clause is restrictive and tells you which pupils are meant, so only the ones at the back are being described — that is what the first version says, not the second. The other two readings contradict never opened and bring in a person the sentence never mentions.
